The occurrence of local moments is widespread in disordered semiconductor materials, such as silicon doped with phosphorus, and it is seen both when these materials are metallic and when they are insulators. We are interested in how this local moment behavior changes as the metal transitions into an insulator. To understand this transition, researchers used advanced computational methods and numerical data to investigate one-dimensional metals and insulators that contain a disorderly distribution of hopping probabilities. They found that even as the system becomes an insulator, it retains characteristics of a metallic state, resulting in logarithmic decline in conductivity at low temperatures. Additionally, the distribution of the interactions between local moments mirrors that of the Borrmann distribution found in random singlet phases. These moments organize into triplets and quartets, and the average size of these groups decreases as power laws at both the metal-insulator transition points. Furthermore, the energy associated with these groups also decreases as power laws, indicating that lower-order groups are the primary magnetic sources even in the insulating state. To confirm these findings, researchers used advanced many-body techniques and exact diagonalization methods to analyze higher-dimensional versions of these systems.

The concept of ordered generating sequences (OGS) was introduced by a group of researchers to extend the applications of Coxeter arrangement theory, allowing for the classification of Coxeter arrangements through their properties, especially in type $A$. In this study, a new type of ordered generating sequence,OGS*-, is developed to better understand Coxeter group bases and has been generalized to types $A$ through $D$.

This study investigates kink soliton patterns within scalar field theory, specifically focusing on the interaction between two real scalar fields. We examine the two-field Lagrangian, which consists of a kinetic term and a potential involving $\mathcal{K}$ and $\mathcal{V}$. By applying an appropriate field redefinition and considering small velocities, we transform the Lagrangian into a more intuitive form and analyze its corresponding equations of motion. We demonstrate that kinematic constraints imposed on $\mathcal{K}$ and $\mathcal{V}$ are necessary for obtaining kinematically constrained kink solutions, which can be represented by a line segment in the field space. We employ a rescaled time and consider small velocities to derive the corresponding equations of motion, which resemble those of a particle moving in an effective potential. We establish a link between the potential's constraints and effective potentials, which determine whether various types of kink solutions exist and discuss a method for classifying these theories accordingly. We derive an expression for the mass of the single massive excitation arising from these theories and a criterion under which the corresponding wave function remains real. We examine the conditions under which the wave function becomes imaginary and interpret this case as an unstable scenario that leads to exponential growth modes. We define the Mas index as an indicator of the number of unstable modes for a given model and provide an example of relevant two-field kink solutions derived from an $O(3)$ symmetric model recently considered, showing that these patterns can

Robots that learn from observation are subject to the constraints of the entities they are observing. A potential workaround is to have the robot infer unobservable control inputs for the observed agent. Existing research in inverse reinforcement learning from trajectories of both controlled and uncontrolled agents has provided valuable insights, yet it has overlooked observable control inputs. We suggest a Bayesian model that allows the robot to leverage information from both controlled and unobservable agents. A key feature is the ability to group similar input behaviors into shared sets and learn from them, which leads to more efficient learning outcomes. We test our model in a 3D version of the game of Tag, which offers a more complex and engaging environment for evaluation, and find that it outperforms a baseline of pre-defined skills by significantly reducing the number of observation trajectories needed.

Given a subgroup $H$ of the fundamental group of a topological space $X$, under what conditions is $X$ considered a strong $H$-transfer space? We will examine the conditions that a covering map $p: X \to B$ must meet in order to be an $H$-transfer, where the fundamental group of the total space $X$ maps onto $H$. Furthermore, given that $X$ is indeed a strong $H$-transfer space, $\pi_n(X)$ will be shown to be a module over the endomorphism ring $\mathcal{E}_H^n(X)$ of the $n$-th homotopy group of $X$.

We introduce a multi-phased deep reinforcement learning strategy to overcome control issues in complex environments. The framework is designed to mitigate two common limitations of deep reinforcement learning, namely sparse and dynamic rewards. To circumvent the issue of sparse rewards, we initially develop a model-predictive control approach to generate basic agent movements within a pre-defined context. Building upon this foundation, we refine this policy through a deep reinforcement learning method in a model-free setting to obtain an optimized action plan. To address the issue of dynamic rewards, we embed a deep set network-based reward prediction network that dynamically adjusts the reward function according to the changing environment. Through thorough evaluation on BENCHMARK, a standardized benchmark for autonomous driving evaluation, our approach effectively tackles control problems under sparse and dynamic reward conditions outperforms existing solutions.

This study is the second part of our investigation into the mass function of black holes over the course of cosmic time. Our primary goal here is to analyze the growth of massive black hole seeds, their ultimate manifestation as extremely massive black holes (both in general and as supermassive black holes), and their formation within the cosmic web's large-scale structure. To achieve this, we employed numerical simulations based on an innovative, self-consistent model for the mass distribution of black holes that we introduced in our first paper. Leveraging our simulations, we tracked the mass of black holes through the cosmic timeline, from their initial formation to their present-day state, and mapped their spatial distribution across the cosmos. Our results show that the majority of the mass in massive black holes originates from a specific type of seed, which forms within massive black holes at extremely high redshifts and is subsequently embedded within massive galaxies, formed within cosmic voids. This finding supports the heavy seed theory of extremely massive black hole formation, and may offer a solution to the discrepancy between the estimated mass and the age of certain extremely massive black holes observed at very high redshifts. Moreover, our simulation-based luminosity function of quasars aligns well with luminosity functions derived from actual quasar surveys, and when combined with the halos in which black holes reside, we find that the quasar luminosity function is naturally "bunched" at shorter wavelengths as a result of black holes' gravitational influence, without the need to consider the

Deep neural networks have been utilized in multiple disciplines to tackle intricate data processing problems, yet their application in inelastic neutron scattering remains largely unexplored. Our research aims to fill this knowledge gap by developing a detailed, reliable, and practical method for employing deep neural networks in solving inelastic neutron scattering issues. We provide an comprehensive explanation of various common problems in this domain and develop corresponding deep neural network solutions. To ensure accuracy and efficiency, we developed specialized tools for data generation, evaluation, and simulation. These tools facilitate a clear and transparent understanding of deep neural network predictions, their scope, and limitations. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach by applying it to two cases: inelastic neutron scattering data analysis and property estimation from limited data. We believe that implementing this technique will contribute to advancements in inelastic neutron scattering, its associated physics models, and relevant materials under investigation.

Over the past three decades, preprints have undergone significant evolution with thirty preprint services having been established and contributing to nearly 800,000 preprints across nearly every area of research. These online platforms provide researchers with the ability to freely and rapidly disseminate their work, an ability that has made preprints the most accessible version of a study to the public, outpacing published articles in a variety of fields. In this report, the preprint landscape is mapped and analyzed through our investigation of the preprint history, global preprint distribution, preprint to published article conversion rates, and the growing impact of preprints across different areas of research. In addition to outlining these findings, we also suggest potential areas for future research in this field and highlight preprints' significant potential to revolutionize information dissemination in science.

In contemporary laboratory settings, meticulous research data management is crucial. Multiple available solutions are either highly tailored or require substantial modification to be effective. This paper introduces a unified solution designed specifically for data-driven investigators working individually or in small groups. Our electronic lab journal is generated automatically from experimental notes and files, subsequently displayed on a website powered by Django. By seamlessly gathering metadata, this system minimizes manual documentation and eliminates errors caused by entering metadata manually. Moreover, the ability to attach files to each log entry minimizes transcription errors. Utilizing a 'lazy' methodology developed within Python, the electronic lab journal is now an established tool used across various research fields.

High-entropy alloys represent an innovative material system architecture where multiple principal elements are combined in equimolar proportions. The complex interactions between these elements give rise to unique properties. Recent advancements utilize machine learning to model the thermodynamic behavior and kinetic constraints within this system. Machine learning offers benefits such as identifying novel HEA compositions with tailored properties and predicting kinetic barriers that may limit their performance. The machine learning approach has the potential to accelerate the development of HEAs as it enables expedited identification of promising candidates.

Assuming the $T_{cc}^+$ discovered at LHCb is a $D^{\ast+}D^0/D^{\ast0}D^+$ hadronic molecule, we investigate the partial decay widths of its charge partner $T_{cc}^+$ into a $D^{\ast+}D\pi$ $D^{\ast0}D\pi$ $D^{\ast0}D^0\pi^+$ and $D^{\ast-}D^0\pi^+$ configuration. The calculation is based on the $SU(3)$ chiral perturbation theory with an non-pointlike form factor that is derived from the $T_{cc}^+$ as a $D^{\ast}D$ hadronic molecule. The $SU(3)$ approach, with the $T_{cc}^+$ model, yields partial decay widths of $\Gamma(K^{\ast0}D^0\pi^+)$ and $\Gamma(K^{\ast-}D^0\pi^+)$ at approximately 10.0 and 1.2 keV, while the $SU(3)$ approach, with the $T_{cc}^+$ model, yields $\Gamma(K^{\ast0}D^0\pi^+)$ and $\Gamma(K^{\ast-}D^0\pi^+)$ at approximately 10.0 and 1.2 ke

Machine learning model design benefits significantly from probability and differential equations in uncovering hidden variables. Gaussian processes and partial differential equations in particular offer robust frameworks, yet combining them into a unified model presents mathematical complexities. This research develops a graph neural network that integrates both probability and differential equation concepts to uncover latent variables within a graph-structured data space. The latent variable space can be perceived as a partial Euclidean space that may possess complex topological characteristics. Our graph neural network utilizes graph signal processing to perform latent variable learning and employs partial differential equations to extend message passing operations onto this hidden space. Compared to existing methods, our approach offers enhanced partial differentiation capabilities and improved representation capabilities for messages. Through rigorous theoretical analysis, we prove that our graph convolutional operator is a valid weak solution to the corresponding partial differential equation, providing more flexibility in the partial differentiation of messages. Additionally, our graph neural network framework exhibits improved capacity for representation messages.

The measure of a vector-valued function's nonlinearity is essentially its distance from affine functions. Researchers have found that the nonlinearity of this type of function with a specific group and codomain is upper bounded by the size of a particular, minimally nonlinear function. They proved that the nonlinearity of a particular type of sparsely populated functions is exactly equal to the maximum possible value, and that this nonlinearity value can be determined by a set of unique differences of a Sidon set. They also found that the nonlinearity value can be expressed as the product of a prime and a positive integer.

Binary matrix sampling with specified row and column sums has a wide array of applications in various fields. This paper presents an efficient algorithm for sampling binary matrices with the required row and column sums at the edge levels, enabling rapid sampling from the corresponding statistical ensemble. Not only does the method support uniform sampling, but it also allows for modified sampling schemes where the probability of an edge being present is a function of the corresponding vertex's degree. We present a theoretical analysis of the algorithm's running time and demonstrate its effectiveness through experiments at various density levels.

Integrating diverse datasets, associated measurement uncertainties and correlated factors into a unified framework enables researchers to derive modified parton distribution functions (PDFs) that better reflect data. A new Python-based framework, the Toldo framework, is developed to facilitate modifications to PDFs according to specified templates of their toldos - quantities representing the difference between measured values and their expected levels without the influence of PDFs. Toldos are obtained by dividing the numerator and denominator of the parton-level cross section expressions by the corresponding nominal cross sections, yielding expressions dependent on kinematic factors and parton distributions. The framework then multiplicatively modifies the individual distribution functions to produce modified PDFs and subsequently recalculates cross sections to derive tellodos. These modified tellodos are compared against the nominal tellodos to quantify the required modifications to the PDFs to match the desired levels. To accommodate the variations in data, weighting factors are introduced to upweight datasets that significantly deviate from the nominal predictions and downweight those that closely match the predictions. Finally, the modified PDFs are obtained by multiplying the nominal PDFs by the changes resulting from the application of the weighted tellodo differences.

This document highlights the latest ELKI version 0.7.5 and provides an overview of its key features as a primary tool for data-driven analysis, including anomaly detection and dimensionality reduction. It also serves as a comprehensive guide with an in-depth algorithm reference section for users.

We've investigated parametric seeding of a microresonator frequency comb using a pump laser with electro-optic-modulated sidebands. The study found that the gap between the pump's sidebands was uniformly transmitted throughout the microresonator, resulting in the direct generation of widely spaced micro-combs. In some cases, the parametric process outperformed the pump's influence, yielding higher micro-comb orders. Additionally, the of the comb lines' intensity and purity increased with the pump's and modulator's powers. In comparison to traditional micro-comb generation methods, significantly reduced optical powers were needed, while the spectrum's resolution and line spacing increased. In the experimental setup described, the micro-comb's micro-spacing increased from 100 MHz to 6.7 GHz with the addition of modulator effects.
We build on existing research by providing evidence that any acylindrically hyperbolic group which admits a non-trivial, faithful invariant random subgroup must be virtually infinite cyclic.

Quantization has been found to improve model performance and reduce computation costs by simulating neural network computations with lower complexity data types. However, most previous research has focused on practical applications rather than providing theoretical backing. We examine a neural network model with quadratic convergence properties (NTK) that uses Rademacher activation and binary weights, and we prove that the QNN based on this model generalizes effectively due to its near-perfect quantization. Furthermore, we break down the influence of binary weights and quantization on the model's global properties, showing the benefits they bring to generalization. Experimentally, we verify the improvements in accuracy and computational efficiency achieved with this model compared to real-valued models, and observe that binary activation networks may generalize poorly, and that extensive quantization can lead to degradation of performance.

Our research builds on previous findings regarding a broad class of bounds that govern bipartite quantum systems and their entanglement entropy. To expand upon this concept, we've expanded its scope to encompass complex quantum circuits known as donut-like configurations and the associated entropy polytopes. By integrating these new configurations, we've identified and developed specific inequalities that guide quantum extremal surfaces. Notably, our work reveals that the dimensions of these inequalities' cones are directly related to the number of constituent parts within respective binary systems, thus expanding on previous theoretical limits.

We've developed a general method to determine the crossing multiplier for solvable lattice models based on any semisimple category, with a particular focus on models derived from a semisimple quadratic Hopf algebras, where the crossing multiplier corresponds to the square of the antipode.

Signal recovery algorithms in compressed sensing often benefit from enhancements 
like stabilization techniques - damping and fractional approaches, which use 
expectation propagation to improve performance and achieve convergence. These 
stabilization methods boost long-term efficiency and enable convergence where 
it wasn't possible before. In this study, we provide an in-depth look at various 
stabilization methods and their effects, comparing their numerical performance and 
showing that a combination of procedures can significantly improve the algorithm.

Miller and Sheffield introduced the concept of an imaginary surface as a pairing of subdomains of the complex plane and associated Gaussian free fields under conformal equivalence. Specifically, they considered the case where these pairings involved chordal multiple Schramm-Loewner evolution (SLE). This paper develops the technical framework necessary to prove that, starting with Gaussian free fields on connected subdomains and choosing appropriate single-sided SLEs, the coupled system remains conformally invariant. We then combine these pairs into the aforementioned coupled system, demonstrating their consistency with Miller-Sheffield's coupling rules for single SLEs. Using these proofs, we establish conformal invariance for the coupled system for both the whole plane and the upper half-plane. We subsequently define the coupled system on the upper half-plane via a limiting process from the coupled system on the whole plane under a family of scaling transformations, thereby proving weak convergence to a stationary distribution that exhibits the expected coupling properties. We also make some observations regarding an related model on the Gaussian free field itself.

In this research, we address the Cauchy problem for the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations in multi-dimensional space with smooth periodic initial conditions and obtain analytical estimates of the solution's maximum norm, tied to the initial conditions' maximum norm.

The concept of quantum complexity has received significant attention in recent years, particularly its relationship to classical complexity classes such as BPP and BQP. Currently, there is a time difference of at most a factor of $n^2$ or $n^3$ that separates the known upper and lower bounds for BQP. In this paper, we establish a new upper bound for the length of quantum circuits that can be verified by classical machines, at a cost of only a factor $n$. Specifically, we demonstrate that there exists a BQP problem, called $\circ$CircuitSat, which can be solved in a time of at most $n \log n$ by a classical machine, but is known to be at least as hard for another BQP problem, called CircuitSat, which can be solved in a time of at most $n$. The key to our finding is a new technique based on quantum walk, which also helps to close a 15-year-old gap in the quantum complexity theory, showing that CircuitSat can be solved in a time of at most $n \log^{O(1)}n$.

Generating synthetic cell shapes that resemble those of cells undergoing apoptosis is a challenging generative task. Achieving this goal requires a significant number of samples for precise modeling due to the diverse range of cell shapes caused by morphological changes during cell death. Traditional generative models utilizing explicit statistical models or pixel-based approaches face difficulties in capturing the complex, irregular shapes of 2D cells. To overcome these limitations, a new implicit representation technique called NeRF is being utilized in this study to create synthetic cell shapes that accurately reflect those undergoing apoptosis. NeRF's effectiveness as a generative model is validated through a series of experiments, including the analysis of generated cell shape distributions and conditional generation capabilities.

Researchers in neuroscience posit that neural systems might utilize specific coordinate systems, such as a 3D Cartesian system, a radial system, or a combined 'log-polar' system, to represent and interpret spatial environments. To evaluate these hypotheses on a broader scale, we collaborated with reinforcement learning experts to create a novel task family. This task, known as gridworlds, can be executed in various spatial representations and allows for the testing of hypotheses using data from both biological and machine learning spatial agents. We've provided the necessary tools to implement our task and analyze results, which will serve as a crucial starting point for understanding how both neural and reinforcement learning agents perceive and interpret spatial information.

To examine the long-term average behavior of complex systems that incorporate complexity, our team has been investigating high-dimensional hard-disk dipoles. These systems are built from numerous particles in high-dimensional space, each consisting of a neutral center and two charged parts. The charged parts interact through long-range electrostatic forces, giving the system a net dipole moment. In this note, we demonstrate that in high dimensions, such as 105 or more, the overall movement of the system in a certain subspace exhibits reversible overall dynamics, despite its dipolar nature, as long as the overall charge distribution remains in a neutral, Gaussian-like state along that subspe, as supported by numerical simulations. This is further verified by numerical evidence that shows slower decay of the system's charge fluctuations in lower dimensions, but still features the same 1/s root-T charge distribution in a 3D space. This finding is significant because it offers a novel approach of restricting the system to a specific subspace to resolve the apparent contradiction between long-range interactions and reversible dynamics, thus offering a simpler and more intuitive explanation than recently proposed for the existence of a diagonal band in the electric spectrum of certain materials. Additionally, our team has generalized this finding to a scenario where the system's dipole is driven by an imbalance in the number of positive and negative charged parts, as long as the system's overall charge distribution remains as described above.

The challenge of Sound Event Localization and Detection involves pinpointing the location and type of distinct sounds occurring in a directional, multi-microphone setup. Recent research primarily relies on complex and computationally intensive methods to achieve precise results. A novel approach utilizing a rectangular Convolutional Recurrent Neural Network has been developed to sound event localization and detection in a more cost-effective setup using 3x3 rectangular filters and by rotating data across multiple channels. Training this network with 128 and 256 sample rates, using the DCASE2020 dataset, has yielded impressive results with a minimum mAP score of 27.77% and maximum mAP score of 31.41%.

In traditional wireless communication, multiple simultaneous transmissions are typically treated as interference and minimized. However, a new approach is gaining attention where wireless systems are designed to simultaneously transmit, while taking advantage of the non-linear characteristics of electronic components and channels at lower power levels. This innovative concept allows for multiple concurrent communications and various coexistence models, as well as applications in ultra-wideband systems and electronic device profiling. This document will provide a comprehensive overview of the research on designing and utilizing wireless systems that transmit simultaneously, focusing on unique air interface designs and alternative coexistence models on the physical, medium access control, and network layers. Additionally, it will explore the concepts of ultra-wideband systems and electronic device profiling as well as provide a glimpse of potential future research directions in this innovative area.

Time-frequency analysis heavily relies on spectrograms, yet their associated level sets, used in visualizing their shape, are not commonly explored in research. To address this, we propose an analytical framework for examining spectrogram level sets in the context of Generalized Gaussian (GGamma) and particularly the Gaussian (Gaussian window, exponent two) signals. Using Gaussian signals as a case study, we apply the properties of Bessel functions to derive explicit formulas for calculating the spectrogram's radial and angular components, which enable us to determine level sets shape in various ways. This includes creating a shape classifier based on type, identifying and locating frequency components of any Gaussian signal, particularly the unknown kernel of a chirp signal, and even applying these methods to non-chirp signals like the Lorentzian and Lorentzian-squared to determine their frequency parameters with high accuracy and robustness.

We've developed a novel universal technique to detect multiple types of dynamic patterns, including stable travelings, as well as complex and synchronized behaviors, in large networks of interacting neurons. Our method relies on the identification of chimeras through a divide-and-conquer approach, which employs a divide-and-conquer idea to progressively increase the resolution of a randomly selected portion of the network until the dynamics of that section are fully decoded. This technique does not require any a-priori knowledge of the network's parameters and can be applied to both continuous and discrete networks. Our results demonstrate the method's robustness in identifying travelings and clustered behaviors, as well as providing a detailed understanding of the network's overall dynamics. Additionally, we use the method to reveal the relationship between the network parameters and the speed of travelings as well as the size of synchronized clusters.

A novel module is presented, allowing researchers to model complex systems influenced by random forces impacting particle motion, a phenomenon anticipated to occur within environments like turbulent planetary disks and the remnants of planetesimal disks. This module streamlines the creation of synchronized noise with variable intensity and auto-correlation time for each particle, with low memory requirements, and is available at no cost through the REBOUNDx supplementary module suite.

Key aspects of quantum science include measurement and feedback, both essential for advanced technologies such as precision measurement and error correction. However, standard tools for analysis fall short in addressing complex feedback loops due to their reliance on pre-determined outcomes. This research presents a new framework for understanding controlled quantum-physical systems, enabling an exact mathematical description of feedback dynamics through a specialized differential equation. This framework is applied to a specifically tuned system for pure amplification and another scenario for computing via quantum stochastic thermal machines, offering insights into optimizing performance during feedback-controlled operation.

In a long and narrow container with horizontal orientation, two types of circular objects with different sizes and weights are placed in an alternating pattern, then subjected to vertical vibrations and horizontal compression. This setup simulates a pack of writing paper in a drawer and is studied using a computational model to understand how the objects settle into a stable arrangement under various conditions such as object density ratios, weight differences, compression and strength levels. This helps to uncover how factors such as object weights and densities affect the final packed arrangement in terms of depth and width.

Research has shown that different flavors of El Ni\~no exhibit distinct global atmospheric patterns associated with extreme precipitation events. We examined how Ni\~no 3 and Ni\~no 4 indices relate to extreme precipitation in the US and Asia, respectively. Although Ni\~no 3 and Ni\~no 4 durations are comparable, Ni\~no 4 Ni\~no 3 ratio is lower during Ni\~no 3 dominant Ni\~no 4 dominant periods. Ni\~no 3 and Ni\~no 4 events have distinct global precipitation patterns, particularly in the Ni\~no 4 dominant Ni\~no 3 dominant periods. Specifically, Ni\~no 4 events are associated with a global belt of very low precipitation at 30-40 degrees latitude, while Ni\~no 3 events are associated with a global belt of very high seasonal precipitation at the same latitudes. Ni\~no 4 events also show an increased global pattern of very low seasonal precipitation at 60-70 degrees latitude, while Ni\~no 3 and Ni\~no 4 dominant Ni\~no 3 dominant periods show no significant difference in this band. Our study emphasizes the importance of considering distinct flavors of El Ni\~no in data analysis, as they have distinct global precipitation patterns.

Recent studies have found that a substantial number of massive black holes can form in isolated, dense clusters which are not part of a larger galaxy. To understand how these black holes end up within galaxies, we need to explore the paths they take, which involve either staying in the dense cluster or migrating to a galaxy due to gravitational interactions. To test the validity of this process, which we call isolated pathway, of isolated black hole formation, the density profile of a host galaxy is compared to that of a ball-dropped cluster. Results for the dwarf galaxy Leo I, which was formed through the isolated pathway, show the presence of an unexpected sub-peak in its density profile. Predictions for other dwarf galaxies, such as Sagittarius, show similar features, which are distinct from those of galaxies that formed through merging, such as the Milky Way. Future observations of these galaxies' densities with the James Webb Space Telescope and other instruments are expected to further confirm this theory.

In systems with electronic flat bands, quantum effects like the negative magnetoresistance (NMR) may arise due to the wave nature of electrons. Research was conducted on a model kagome metal incorporating three types of electrons, and it was found that the presence of all three can induce flat bands, thus generating the NMR phenomenon in the system's ground state. The negative resistance becomes less pronounced at elevated temperatures and decreases in strength with increased electron-hole interaction. The NMR is found to be robust against structural imperfections but is significantly impacted by magnetic disorder, and its magnitude is found to be proportional to the carrier density, opening up the possibility of utilizing this property in sensor technology.

Understanding how specific genetic variations affect traits and diseases through genomic pathways is a complex task.  Identifying crucial genetic factors (causative cis-regulatory elements, CREs) involved in a disease process can be a challenging task, especially with the advent of massive data sets from genome-wide association studies (GWAS) that pinpoint many influential genetic variations.  However, with the advent of data-integration techniques, it is now possible to leverage both chromatin activity data (CAD) and GWAS data to determine CREs' impact on traits.  A joint analysis of CAD and GWAS allows for the selection of variations supported by CAD within genomic regions associated with a disease, thereby helping researchers to identify causative genetic factors.  Combining CAD, annotation, and Bayesian learning can further help researchers to determine the effects of regulatory variations.  As such, this study aims to provide an in-depth examination of this issue, by conducting an extensive joint analysis of 4T2 cadmium-treated, human induced pluripotent cells (hiPSCs), CAD, and GWAS data of 18 traits, thereby contributing valuable insights into the effects of genetic variations.  With the advent of massive data sets, researchers now face a myriad of data integration and analysis issues, including data quality, appropriate data selection, and avoiding correlations that appear to be causal but are actually coincidental.  To address these concerns, this study proposes a data-integration technique that combines CAD, annotation, and GWAS

This study identifies and classifies 2-designs that satisfy specific conditions and have specific automorphism properties. A non-trivial 2-design's automorphism group can either be an subgroup of the alternating group or a specific type of group associated with a simple group in the list.

This study examines electronic correlation within confined hydrogen, helium and lithium ions in their base states using entropy measures. Different wavefunctions are used to better account for inter-electronic interactions. The resulting entropy values show sensitivity to these interactions. In situations of extremely tight confinement, Coulomb effects are minimized and models treating particles as independent or non-interacting pairs in an identical state accurately interplay correlation. Energy estimates derived from these models are inagreement with existing literature.

The velocity distribution of wide binary stars is a widely used test to evaluate modified gravity theories. However, its application has been limited by the lack of comprehensive data. In this research, we analyze the velocity distribution of 11,000 wide binary stars within 70 parsecs of the sun, obtained from high-precision Gaia data. Our findings reveal the presence of a line at a velocity difference of approximately 25 km/s, which is consistent with earlier studies. The origin of this line is attributed to the Gaia's selection bias, rather than modified gravity, and our discovery provides the first quantitative evidence of such a bias. Furthermore, we establish that the amplitude of this bias is parameterized by a characteristic velocity and identify the necessary conditions under which a wide binary data set can be utilized to constrain modified gravity theories.

To each multiplicative linear logic proof structure, we relate an ideal that encapsulates its logical meaning through polynomial equations. We demonstrate how cut-elimination in multiplicative proof nets parallels specific applications of the Buchberger algorithm, a method used for computing Gröbner bases in elimination theory.

This work introduces a novel approach to forecasting the synchronization status of time series from different sectors. Given the intricate nature of underlying cross-system dynamics, the proposed method focuses on approximating future cross-recurrence behavior by leveraging historical cross-recurrence patterns. To quantify synchronization, we utilize financial time series and measure the overlap between the combined recurrence rate of two series and their individual rates. Our approach involves employing a deep learning model, specifically a Convolutional Neural Network, to predict cross-recurrence characteristics and evaluate synchronization status. We validate our method using European stock market data from three countries, demonstrating the model's ability to predict cross-country synchronization with a 1-day prediction horizon and achieving over 70% prediction accuracy.

THz radiation enables the precise manipulation of electronic, phononic, and excitonic components within materials. This precise manipulation permits the investigation of the interplay between electrons and lattice vibrations, which significantly influences material properties. In this research, we present comprehensive electron-phonon and spin-phonon interaction data obtained from a detailed study of the spin-orbital fluctuations in LAO/STO superlattices under various infrared and THz pulse stimuli. Notably, our findings reveal that certain phononic modes, which are initially activated, later give rise to a spin-wave response. This phenomenon is attributed to spin-phonon coupling, as opposed to direct electronic coupling. Furthermore, by introducing an analogy between inertia and electron-phonon coupling, we propose a new model, illustrating that a phonon-driven spin wave effect can be explained. This contribution provides a framework for manipulating spin textures through spin-phonon coupling, potentially paving the way for the development of phononic spintronic devices.

Delivery of click-through rate (CTR) predictions to ad platforms is a critical component in determining ad display. Leveraging ad features and historical user-ad interactions, ad models can predict the likelihood of user clicks. Nonetheless, leveraging text-based features alone is often insufficient to boost CTR predictions. To enhance these predictions, visual ad content should also be considered. Nonetheless, utilizing visual cues presents several obstacles, including the difficulty in accurately detecting user ad interactions via visual means and efficiently processing visual data. To overcome these difficulties, we introduce content-aware neural networks (CANets), a family of vision-and-language models designed to improve CTR predictions by leveraging visual content. Canonical in nature, CANets utilize neural encoding to content visual ad components and orthogonal neural networks to model user ad interactions via visual cues. To effectively leverage visual content and overcome data imbalance issues, we employ canonical neural networks to model user ad interactions via visual cues and employ contrastive learning to enhance content matching. Through experimentation with 14 real-world datasets, we demonstrate that CANets surpass existing state-of-the-art models utilizing language-only cues by approximately 3.1 points in terms of AUC scores.

Business Process Case Models that track the state of business entities called Cases provide essential information about processes. In this study, we incorporate a specific type of restriction, known as cardinality constraints, into these models to accurately reflect the limited number of instances that businesses typically create. This integration enables the development of a new type of analysis, referred to as bounded-checking, which determines if a given case model adheres to these constraints. To achieve this, we convert the given checks into specific mathematical representations, or bounded check systems, and then employ an iterative method to create and analyze these models for their adherence to these constraints.

Wildfires are a natural phenomenon that significantly impacts the global biosphere and atmosphere through the release of harmful particulate matter, known as PM, which in turn affects climate and air quality while reducing visibility and threatening human health and aviation safety. Understanding how large-scale wildfire aerosols are formed is essential to accurately assess their distribution, transport, and overall effects. This paper presents a physics-based statistical model that leverages multi-source infrared data from geostationary satellites to monitor and analyze the combustion process of wildfire aerosols in real-time. By harnessing a combination of data-driven and physics-informed methods, the model achieves a precise estimation of key parameters including combustion intensity, heat release rates, and PM emission rates across different chemical species. Extensive case studies using California and Australia wildfires demonstrate the model's ability to provide accurate, continuous observations of fire behavior and understand underlying physical processes, thereby significantly advancing real-time wildfire monitoring and real-time air quality forecasting systems.

Protecting users of location-based services with significant privacy requirements is extremely difficult when multiple locations are shared within a short time frame due to the significant relationships anticipated between these locations. Our proposed R\'enyi divergence based framework measures and bounds expected privacy losses for interrelated data sets, further demonstrated through an algorithm incorporating conditional Gaussian process priors. This framework illustrates the challenges in safeguarding dependent data and provides a strategic approach to maintaining significant privacy when multiple dependent locations are shared.

Research has shown that analyzing connectivity within large brain networks from resting-state fMRI data from multiple sites can be challenging due to site-specific variability, which may mask true connectivity patterns. A study was conducted to evaluate how connectivity estimates from resting-state fMRI data, which can be influenced by analysis methods and site effects, are affected when combining data from multiple sites. Using simulated time-series and real multi-echo imaging data from multiple sites, the statistical power and prediction accuracy of connectivity estimates were tested. The results revealed that using resting-state fMRI data from multiple sites simultaneously can lead to overestimation of connectivity and inaccurate model performance. The randomness of participants and physiological factors such as heart rate influenced the connectivity estimates. The results suggest that resting-state fMRI can be used to study large-scale brain networks at an individual level, but using data from multiple sites in the same analysis can lead to inaccuracies. The findings have potential implications for understanding psychiatric and neurodegenerative disorders that may exhibit altered brain connectivity.

Building on previous work, where a directed graph equivalent of the Ricci curvature was developed based on the Chung Laplacian, this note focuses on deriving a characterization of our lower Ricci curvature bound by applying a heat semigroup gradient estimate and a heat flow-based transportation inequality. This will serve as the basis for establishing a concentration of measure inequality for directed graphs with positive Ricci curvature.

Recent advances in NLP for code-mixed texts have been limited to multilingual models that are not always efficient or transparent. To address this, we propose a novel lightweight encoder-adapter framework called PESTO, which dynamically processes input tokens based on their language using a switching encoding technique. The framework's encoding and matching techniques ensure that tokens' position and language-specific characteristics are effectively captured. Evaluations on Hindi-English code-mixing show that PESTO outperforms strong multilingual and monolingual baselines on tasks like pseudo-translation and sentiment analysis, while being at least as resource-efficient as its counterparts.

Using a combination of density functional theory and density functional perturbation theory, we studied the phonon spectrum and electronic structure of Tc in H3S hydride as a function of pressure and isotope mass. Numerical results show that the Fermi level shifts with increasing pressure, leading to the emergence of a van Hove singularity at higher pressures. The position of the van Hove singularity relative to the Fermi level has a significant impact on the isotope effect, with the exponent changing from 0.27 to 0.32 when crossing the singularity. Beyond 222 GPa, the exponent begins to decrease again, with our findings agreeing with previous theoretical predictions.

Fisher's average effect is a fundamental concept in the inference of causal relationships from observational data, and this article provides a theoretical foundation for this idea. We first establish that under the conditions of conditional d-separation and the closure of a set of variables, Fisher's average effect equates to both a direct causal effect and a post-stratification effect. Furthermore, these causal properties can be utilized to establish a version of the b-consistency postulate proposed by Robins.

This research proposes a visual relocalization technique based on geometric information derived from 3D surfel mapping. A comprehensive database of images is initially created, linking 2D image features to 3D geometric entities via global indices obtained through mapping rendering. By applying surfel reprojection, a set of candidate locations is identified from sensor observations, which guides the selection of image features that are both association and metricically plausible. A neural descriptor-based feature matching algorithm is leveraged to refine this candidate pool, ultimately yielding high precision and robustness across diverse environments and scales变化. A rigorous evaluation is conducted using novel, real-world datasets representing diverse scenes, demonstrating the method's efficacy in various conditions including dramatic scale variations and significant pose changes.

Decentralized learning technique, federated learning, and data that lacks
annotation lead to optimization of semi-centralized loss functions, which
results in suboptimal outcomes due to remaining variable data variance. To
overcome this limitation, we develop an alternative approach that directly
optimizes the variance of remaining data and thus minimizes optimization
uncertainty on the remaining hypothesis. This approach is achieved through
an alternating optimization method that successively minimizes the variance
of remaining data and updates the shared model parameters. Building upon this
concept, we design a personalization technique using local data, which helps
overcome the overfitting issue during variance minimization and shared model
update. Experimental verification using well-known benchmark datasets shows
that variance reduction significantly improves variation of remaining data
and optimization efficiency. Furthermore, our personalization method surpasses
several state-of-the-art approaches in terms of accuracy and generalizability
on the benchmark datasets.

We simulate second-long black hole-neutron star merges in a radiative, magnetized environment, examining the effect on the final neutron star's equation of state, the binary spin, the initial magnetic field within each neutron star, and the magnetic field within the interstellar disk that surrounds them. The simulation shows that the mass of the neutron star remnant can be up to ten percent heavier than it would be in a non-radiative, non-magnetized scenario, with the effect of magnetic field and radiative pressure combining to produce this result. The impact of initial conditions on the remnant mass is significant, with a ten percent increase possible, while the final neutron star's equation of state may also experience a two percent increase. Notably, the neutron star's equation of state has little to no effect on the final remnant mass. Furthermore, the mass ejected during the merge is up to ten times greater in a radiative, magnetized simulation than in standard simulations, with the effect of initial conditions accounting for additional variability. The impact of initial conditions on mass ejection is substantial, with a factor of two increase possible. The energy and angular momentum carried away by neutrinos also experience increases of up to ten percent and twenty percent, respectively. The impact of magnetic field on remnant mass and mass ejection is substantial, with a ten percent and twenty percent increase possible for strong fields and a soft equation of state, while this impact is substantially smaller for stiffer equations of state.

A novel variation of the Kawazumi-Zhang invariant, specifically $\varphi(C)$,
for compact Riemann surfaces $C$ of genus $g \geq 1$ is presented, exploring
its connections to the first Mumford-Morita-Miller class $e_1 = \kappa_1$ on the
moduli space and its relation to the traditional Kawazumi-Zhang invariant.

This note primarily focuses on measuring the speed of a conditioned process approaching its quasi-stationary equilibrium under specific assumptions regarding its distribution. In reverse, we are able to quantify the convergence speed of the conditioned process when its initial distribution does not necessarily align with the characteristics of a domain or its Martin boundary. This is achieved by establishing a relationship, in the form of an upper bound, between the domain's principal eigenfunction and its projection onto the space of 1 and the exponential of the rate of convergence generator. As a consequence, we are able to derive an asymptotic representation of the eigenfunction at points nearing the domain's boundary. This result can be further applied to a variety of examples including those in higher dimensions and those with boundaries defined by a random or deterministic factor.

This research explores the optical interaction between a dimer of dielectric nanoparticles and a graphene sheet, focusing on how the graphene's surface plasmons excite in the optical range. An accurate analytical expression has been developed to quantify the optical force acting on the particles, which enables the identification of a condition under which the particles become bound by the excitation of the graphene's surface plasmons. Specifically, this phenomenon occurs within a certain frequency range of the graphene's surface plasmons, typically in the terahertz or infrared area. Additionally, it was found that the surface plasmon binding effect is more pronounced for smaller particles and can be more effectively achieved for larger particles when their separation from the graphene sheet is increased. For instance, 50-nm silica particles can be bound at an exc wavelength of 1.55 $\mu$m with an optimal distance of around 200 nm from the graphene. This novel phenomenon of plasmon binding offers potential for the development of new methods to manipulate nanoparticles and could also lead to the creation of compact, frequency-selective optical traps that utilize plasmons.

To minimize patient harm and reduce overcrowding in treatment, we must understand how long emergency department (ED) visits typically last. The length of visits depends on several factors, including the patient's condition, which we can measure using a standardized triage system. To get a clear picture of visit durations, we must develop a statistical model that accounts for variations in patient characteristics. The type of treatment an patient receives also influences visit length, so we should express emergency department waiting times in two parts: (1) a type-specific duration and (2) changes due to different patient types. The second component can be modeled using a common framework, but the first requires a model that accounts for two types of interactions: how different patient characteristics affect treatment, and how an patient's condition influences treatment choice. The type of treatment an patient receives, including resuscitation, resuscitation with monitoring, treatment, reevaluation, and diagnostic, also impacts wait times, so we should express emergency department waiting times in two parts: (1) a type-specific duration and (2) changes due to different patient types in the first part and (3) reevaluation and diagnostic

In cooperative systems with multiple tasks, the concept of strategic multi-task coordination involves each agent selecting a task and producing output to gain a reward, and is modeled by a game where each participant's payoff depends on their own and others' tasks and actions. By using a network of computational units with fixed, unidirectional connections that facilitate regular communication, each unit performs regular updates of a common parameter and a parameter dependent on its position, and uses these to guide their connected unit. Through this mechanism, agents can self-organize into patterns, and we show that such systems can converge to strategic multi-task coordination equilibria under conditions of regular computation and communication.

Research into the chiral magnetic effect in heavy-ion collisions can be investigated by analyzing charge-dependent particle flow patterns. This study provides the first measurement of this phenomenon, where the influence of magnetic field direction was considered, using data from Pb-Pb collisions from the ALICE experiment. The measurements of second- and third-order flow patterns, which are charge-dependent, revealed that the V-shaped flow pattern dominates over other effects and that the chiral magnetic effect's contribution is negligible compared to other effects at 2.76 and 5.02 TeV collisions.

The surge in online fundraising platforms has enabled the online crowd to influence organizations' decision-making through communicated signals. Understanding the online crowd's signals that signal association with funded projects is the focus of our research. To achieve this, our team conducted an extensive study across three distinct online platforms, each with unique characteristics and features. By aggregating and analyzing this empirical data, our findings indicate that specific signal categories are associated with funded projects on all platforms. Additionally, specific signal within each category demonstrate platform-specific importance for projects that received funding. Ultimately, our study contributes to the understanding of online crowd behavior and its impact on organizations' decision-making.

Machine learning-based system security is significantly impacted by data myopia and information silos. Artificial intelligence (AI)-driven network security, in particular, faces difficulties when making inferences in real-world scenarios due to a lack of comprehensive, representative data. Traditional centralised models, however, pose data privacy risks and create technical barriers to in-depth, comprehensive knowledge of local network security, resulting in data ownership issues and trust deficits. To address these challenges, a fully distributed federated learning model is proposed, allowing multiple network nodes to train and create a collaborative, robust malware detection model without exchanging raw data. A comprehensive simulation using a Network Normalization and Malware Generation (FLORE) platform demonstrates the effectiveness of federated learning in creating malware detection models and outperforms centralised models despite training with smaller local datasets.

The issue of scheduling a robot's tasks to minimize movement time is a long-standing problem in manufacturing. Our study focuses on a specific version of this problem, where a robot moves between multiple fixed positions at the same height. To solve this challenge, we initially examine the theoretical underpinnings of two approximation algorithms derived from the Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP). However, these algorithms were impractical to apply in a real-world scenario due to their high computational demands. Therefore, we developed two new, finite-state approximation algorithms, leveraging the hierarchical structure of tasks. The first algorithm employs a single pass through the tasks to determine the optimal sequence, while the second employs clustering techniques to group tasks and schedule them efficiently. The performance of these algorithms was tested against two benchmark instances, revealing favorable comparisons to a commercial programming software's performance.

The performance of the interface between semiconductors and insulators is crucial for the operation of advanced electronic devices, particularly advanced SiMOSFETs. This study employs a combination of Atomic Force Microscopy (AFM) and Electrostatic Force Microscopy (EFM) to investigate SiMOSFET gate insulation quality and mobility. To achieve this goal, we investigated the effects of thermal treatment, hydrogen plasma treatment, and the introduction of a buffer layer on SiO2 gate insulation. These treatments were applied to SiMOSFETs fabricated in an advanced 300mm CMOS process. Thermal treatment alone yielded significant improvements in mobility and interface quality. However, incorporating hydrogen and silicon carbide further enhanced mobility and interface parameters in more advanced devices. This research also compares numerical simulations with experimental data to validate the findings.

In a network of interconnected oscillators divided into groups, we examine how synchronization occurs despite varying parameters within the oscillators, by analyzing the stability of the system's most synchronized state. The most synchronized state corresponds to a situation where every oscillator within each group moves in perfect unison, resulting in $N-$ clusters of oscillations, where $N$ represents the number of groups. A particular type of hyperbolic stability is required for synchronization to occur within each group, and we explore the impact of weaker connections between the oscillators within each group, and those between the groups, on this stability. Our research reveals that, due to weaker intra-group connections, the condition for hyperbolic stability can be decoupled into separate conditions for each group, and that groups can achieve independent synchronization despite interactions with other groups and parameter discrepancies within the oscillators.

Our study examines whether video search results are biased towards limiting
source diversity. To investigate this, we use a virtual agent search framework,
which allows us to conduct a search audit by using diverse query combinations.
The framework employs an LLM-based video agent that leverages semantic word
embeddings to generate relevant subqueries. We apply this framework to audit the
top five English video search engines, analyzing result sources, ranks and
recurrence rates. The findings indicate that both recursive and sequential
searches using virtual agents often lead to a limited set of top video search
engines, with a dominant platform accounting for a disproportionate number of
results. Moreover, our study also highlights a video diversity issue, as the
content of both individual and combined search results tends to focus on video
games and tutorials, while other genres like news and educational videos are
underrepresented.

To gain insight into Monodromy defects in conformal field theories, we compute various characteristics of the Wess-Zumino model to its second order accuracy. These features include asymptotic data, conformal cross-ratios, and a function called $\mathcal{F}$, all related to four-point conformal block compositions. By analyzing the behavior of these quantities under a regime where one scaling dimension approaches another, we derive the precise form of this function in relation to its underlying CFT data. Furthermore, we verify our findings by directly integrating the relevant equations for a specific theoretical model.

This paper focuses on a Medium Access Control (MAC) framework for randomly accessing a network and evaluates correlation-based interference in the network's transmit opportunities. We introduce the concept of interference correlation and derive its statistical characteristics. Our findings indicate that random access can reduce interference but increase uncertainty in opportunities. To address these challenges, we develop an interference model that considers the effects of interference correlation and imperfect interference management. Using this model, a theoretical model of network capacity with consideration for interference correlation is created. We then create an optimal interference management method to minimize the cost of managing interference and utilize the Lagrange multiplier method to create an efficient, sub-optimal interference management method that only manages a single parameter. A numerical analysis is also conducted to illustrate the impact of interference correlation on the efficiency of different interference management methods and to compare our sub-optimal interference management method with an optimal interference management method that takes into consideration the number of interference parameters.

Using graph neural networks (GNNs) with a small amount of labeled data is challenging due to the need for a large amount of labels for effective supervised learning. To overcome this limitation, we use a combination of pseudo-labeling (PL) and pseudo-contrastive learning (PCL) to enhance the performance of GNNs when trained with limited labeled and abundant unlabeled data. Specifically, PL generates labels for unlabeled data based on a trained model's output, while PCL selects high-quality pseudo-labels based on similar nodes with high-confidence predictions. Informative pseudo-labels are then used as a supervision signal for both labeled and unlabeled data to improve model performance. Our proposed method Informative Pseudo-Contrastive Learning (IPL) selects the highest quality pseudo-labels using a node's and its neighbor's representation similarity, and uses a cross-modal contrastive loss to align the features of both labeled and pseudo-labeled data. Our approach has been shown to outperform state-of-the-art methods on three graph datasets with limited labels, and ablation studies have validated the effectiveness of our method's key components.

Video processing tasks such as coding and compression heavily rely on efficient reference image selection, but current methods often involve computationally expensive operations. Introducing PatchNet, a novel, template-matching approach that leverages patch-based analysis and machine learning to efficiently identify key frames. By focusing on a local area, these networks can accurately select an optimal template with up to 100 times fewer operations, while retaining over 90% of the performance of the best existing methods. Our results from large-scale simulations on diverse video content demonstrate the success of PatchNet in real-time applications, achieving a 40% improvement in compression over a patch-matching baseline, and a significant performance gain of up to 20 bits per lambda over a fully-convolutional neural network method, all with substantial computational savings.

We have exact expressions for the joint distribution of particle positions at different times in the discrete time periodic asymmetric simple exclusion process. This is in addition to the known results for continuous time periodic asymmetric exclusion process at various scales of observation, which were previously obtained using the continuous limit approach. Our results fill in the gap by providing a pairwise correlation function and a full $n$-point joint distribution for the discrete time periodic model.

A new approach to wireless networks is proposed, considering a frequency division duplex (FDD) system that integrates multiple services and simultaneous wireless information and energy transfer (SWIPT). To address the challenges posed by network interference and energy reception limits, an optimized power allocation algorithm based on block coordinate descent (BCD) is developed to maximize the network's spectral efficiency. The problem is divided into downlink and uplink sub-problems, each further decomposed into more manageable energy maximization and interference minimization tasks. Specifically, one sub-problem can be efficiently resolved using convex optimization, while the other is tackled with an iterative optimization technique that gradually refines the solution by alternating service and user resource allocation. The resulting algorithm demonstrates strong convergence, stability, and convergence performance in simulations, revealing significant performance gains and at least a 50% reduction in switch iterations compared to a time division duplex (TDD) baseline after the network stabilizes.

For quantum systems that exhibit a high degree of symmetry, it is often assumed that characteristics that are independent of specific details can be predicted with precision. This study examines the validity of this assumption for Pauli-exclusion-principled Fermi gases, that is, a principle that limits how many identical fermions can occupy a single quantum state. By simulating N-component Fermi gases using the lattice Boltzmann method, we found that the non-interacting and weakly repulsive regimes exhibit distinct behaviors, which is in contrast to the assumption of universality. This discovery is particularly relevant to research on ultra-cold Fermi gases, where it helps to clarify the effects of repulsive interactions. Furthermore, we developed a theoretical model based on the non-interacting limits and made predictions for the first time on how certain key parameters, such as compressibility and speed of sound, evolve as the number of components (N) increases.

We develop a generic model for electro-mechanical systems that can also describe traditional microwave optomechanical interactions. The total energy of these systems is described through three components: the kinetic energy of the vibrating element, the storage of electric and magnetic fields, and their respective interactions. By applying these fundamental principles, we derive a linear circuit model incorporating a variable inductor that accurately captures the optomechanical interaction. Using this simplified model, we can simulate the behavior of complex microwave optomechanical systems similar to how a circuit with linear and variable circuit elements describes a mechanically induced optomechanical system. Furthermore, we apply our model to electrically driven systems and both scenarios are used to single-mode quantum dynamics analysis.

Properties of semi-classical orthogonal polynomials relative to a generalized Airy weight and their corresponding zeros and recurrence coefficients are examined, where specific parameters apply. The study extends to a symmetrized form of this weight known as the generalized sextic Freud weight, resulting in a parallel investigation of the associated polynomials' properties.

This study examines a wall-following robot's behavior as it navigates a room with a simple intersection, focusing on how changes in the robot's turning tendency affect its motion. This demonstration uses a simple robot model and can serve as a tangible illustration of a fundamental concept in the theory of dynamical systems, specifically the emergence of complex behavior from simple rules. By altering a key parameter in the robot's control mechanism, this investigation demonstrates how the robot transitions through a series of dynamic regimes, ultimately resulting in unpredictable motion.

This article further develops the concepts of algebra and symmetry within 2d fermionic quantum field theory, focusing on specific types of interactions represented by polynomial interactions. The study reveals that the initial algebra, suitable for preserving certain symmetries, has a broader classification when these specific interactions are involved. As a result, a broader category of algebraic quantum field theories can be established. The article then leverages this classification to study the properties of free scalar field, demonstrating that it exhibits chiral currents within its underlying algebra. The concept of a "chiral half-symplectic form" is also introduced to facilitate this study. The article then begins examining real interactions within this context.

Laparoscopic surgery relies on a smoke evacuation system to maintain visibility of internal components and instruments within the abdominal cavity, as smoke produced during laser-induced surgical procedures can obstruct the camera's view. To address this challenge, a machine learning-based smoke detection system is proposed, which uses a lapping camera's images to identify smoke regardless of the lighting conditions. A key component of this system is an image enhancement technique that enhances low-quality, laparoscopic camera images by artificially increasing their brightness and contrast. Experimental results demonstrate that applying image enhancement significantly improves the smoke detector's performance by increasing its accuracy and reducing false positives.

This research focuses on creating resilient Molmer-Sorensen gates using trapped ions arranged in a line, incorporating Gaussian amplitude modulation and a careful balance of motion frequency effects. We demonstrate the gate's performance through simulations of experimental frequencies, and propose an optimal scheme that outmatches a previously known algorithm in meeting fidelity requirements. Additionally, the need for precise frequency knowledge is significantly reduced, making the production of Molmer-Sorensen gates more feasible.

Using advanced computer simulations, researchers investigated how a specific type of atomic arrangement contributes to a certain type of crystal structure and its transition to a different structure. Their analysis revealed that this particular arrangement does not significantly influence how the atoms move in the desired structure, but rather how a different, more stable atomic arrangement does. Additionally, they found that the way a material transforms from a symmetric structure to a more complex one is directly related to the way a specific atomic group tilts in the most stable material form, supporting a theory that explains this transformation. These findings can be used to predict the way similar materials will behave in an unexpected manner.

Multivariate data that vary over a continuum are often analyzed using Functional Gaussian Graphical Models (FGGs) or Graphical Gaussian Processes (GGPs), both of which employ a kernel function. In this research, we establish that FGGs can be seen as a type of GGP, using a specific spectral approximation based on the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of the kernel's Gram matrix. However, due to this approximation, FGGS will not precisely match the GGP specification, leading to some implicit differences. In contrast, previous research has shown that GGGs can be represented as Functional Gaussian Graphical Models through different approximations, such as discretization or the spectral method. These findings highlight a slight asymmetry in the relationship between FGGs and GGPs, as well as providing insights into the inherent connections between these methods and future directions for exploration.

Existing quantum processors are prone to systematic errors growing with distance from the control circuit's center due to variations in qubit control and connections. To minimize these errors, crucial quantum algorithms need to be compiled into the smallest possible subquadratic square size on a $q \times q$ grid, where $q = O(\sqrt{n})$. However, no efficient compilation method exists for almighty grids that handle a wide range of essential quantum algorithms. In this research, we develop a new family of efficient quantum circuit compilers with subquadratic complexities, capable of compiling fundamental patterns such as nested loops, collective control, and more, by introducing a general compiler for fundamental patterns and optimal compilers for specific applications like Grover's search and the quantum Fourier transform.

A recent approach to optimizing techniques employs average-case analysis, enabling more precise performance predictions than traditional worst-case assessments. However, leveraging this analysis comes with a significant drawback: verifying assumptions requires intricate, computationally expensive, and non-robust algorithms. We address this challenge in the context of convex optimization, showcasing that average-case assessments of key algorithms like Gradient Descent, Accelerated Gradient, and Aggregation of Algorithms remain valid without specific assumptions. Moreover, we establish that these algorithms are approximately 1-stable, indicating approximately the same level of robustness as Algorithms in Visions in Optimization (AVIOs). We also examine the implications of this finding on differential privacy, discovering that average-case analyses of Algorithms in Visions in Optimization often lead to tighter privacy guarantees.

We used numerical methods to study the excitation spectrum of a two-layer excitonic insulator.
Starting with a model derived from the non-interressing band structure, we applied
the self-consistent T-matrix approach to handle strong interactions between
electrons in a lattice system, which enabled us to explore the excitation
properties of this two-layer system.
Our calculations revealed a distinctive change in the excitation spectrum at zero
energy when a non-zero density of states at the Fermi level is present,
characteristic of a two-layer system in this state,
which agrees with the behavior of a continuous liquid system.
Additionally, at zero momentum, the excitation energy approaches zero with a
power of three times the momentum,
while in a single-layer system the excitation energy goes as the square root of the
momentum.
These results show that the collective fluctuations in this two-layer system
behave like a phonon-like boson, with a non-zero quasi-particle gap,
which we interpret as a spin-wave like phonon.
We also studied the optical conductivity of this two-layer system,
which displays a Drude-like peak at zero frequency and an associated quasi-particle
gap, which we suggest may be measured using transport experiments.

We have developed a message-passing algorithm designed to accurately determine the location and track of mobile devices, even in the presence of abnormal signal conditions. The solution we designed addresses the issue of non-linear, noisy observations in a decentralized system with multiple receivers, all of which are designed to minimize the error in tracking. The algorithm automatically adjusts its operation under both normal and abnormal signal conditions and considers the impact of asymmetric measurement noise. The approach also has the added benefit of providing accurate results with a relatively low computational cost. The solution we designed is particularly useful in the context of radio-based localization and tracking, which is critical for the safe operation of autonomous vehicles and other advanced technologies. The theoretical underpinnings and performance of the solution we designed are substantiated by the results of numerical analysis and real-world experiments.
