In the context of topological string theory, this research examines topological T-duality on typical torus backgrounds with twisted boundary conditions, referred to as twisted tori or foliated spaces. The study derives key invariants for these twisted tori, specifically low-energy symmetries and K-theory groups of B-fields, employing explicit representations of the double group $\tilde G$ associated with the holonomy group $G$ of the twisted geometry, which can be either discrete torsion or generalised moment maps. The findings are supported by findings for topological K-theory and T-duality of non-compact twisted spaces.

In Co-Imitation Learning (CIL), multiple agents learn by observing a variety of expert shows, with each show corresponding to a single action executed by the experts.  Since there are often limited numbers of shows available, overfitting becomes a significant challenge for the agents.  Our proposed method addresses this limitation by enabling the agents to learn from one another through observation, effectively allowing them to supplement their limited expert observations with data gathered through inter-agent interaction.  By providing richer expert data with fewer demonstrations, our approach outperforms traditional Imitation Learning and other state-of-the-art reinforcement learning techniques on the Bridge game environment.

This paper investigates properties of Plain Azimuthal Codes (PACs), focusing on their use in flatbed imprint processes for micro and nano imprinting techniques. PACs are a type of two-dimensional periodic pattern that exhibits a specific symmetry around the vertical axis. Our analysis reveals that the set of all possible PACs with point group $C_n^{\infty}$ forms a closed subset within the space of all two-dimensional periodic patterns. We establish a connection between PACs and the flatbed imprinting of periodic microstructures, demonstrating that any target structure that can be fabricated using印印 process can also be designed using PACs in a compatible way. Our metric allows us to quantify how closely a PAC approximates a given periodic structure, and is shown to be equivalent to considering only vertical cross-sections of the patterns in the flatbed imprinting context. Furthermore, we develop an efficient algorithm for finding the optimal PAC within a given equivalence class, which significantly reduces computational complexity when searching for optimal quasicrystalline patterns.

This project focuses on recovering hand and object poses from unstructured 3D point cloud sequences that depict interactions between them.
Initially, our approach tracks hand objects as they move within an environment to generate a rough hand and object trajectory, which we then utilize to synchronize hand and object motion into a single timestamped sequence.
Next, our network accurately predicts dense, smooth, and physically plausible deformations of objects, even when they are deformed, by leveraging both a learned model of object appearance and the trajectory information.
We extensively test our method on diverse real-world sequences, including those involving a range of deformed objects, which are independently captured, and observe object transformation patterns to identify object instances without requiring specific training.
Finally, our method can be applied to generate a DECODED video, which highlights object deformation and provides a framework to train a decoder that can translate a deformed object back to its original shape, given just a deformed point cloud.
We also explore the potential to reconstruct DECODED objects from a single captured hand-object interaction point cloud.

This study employs the modular reduction technique to a Coxeter group of rank 4 featuring a star diagram with 5, 3, and k= 3, 4, 5, or 6 labels, using the odd primes from the ring Z[tau], where tau represents the golden ratio. It categorizes each reduced group as a reflection group over a finite field and demonstrates that the reduced group retains its properties regardless of the used prime in the reduction process.

A novel, markerless extrinsic calibration system is introduced that utilizes a training dataset and a convolutional neural network to identify and track a robot's end-effector pose without the need for physical markers, using only a depth camera. Our approach's innovation lies in employing a neural network for extrinsic calibration, leveraging training data to learn a direct mapping between a depth camera's image and a end-effector pose. The system's performance is enhanced by incorporating a training dataset, which can be generated using a simulated environment, ensuring substantial improvements over markerless systems with limited training data. A simulated training environment is introduced to facilitate the generation of a training dataset, and the performance of our system is evaluated on a real-world setup, demonstrating superior performance compared to an alternative system lacking training data.

A new model is developed to understand treatment interference in units that interact with each other over limited ranges. This model enables researchers to formulate hypotheses about these interactions and develop methods to test them empirically. The theoretical framework of the model is grounded in set theory and offers a broader scope than previously used approaches. The models of Rubin (2001) and Aronovich and Muñiz (2019) are specifically encompassed within this framework. The proposed approach involves utilizing the K-nearest-neighbor comparison units to estimate the effects of treatment and assessing the validity of these effects through examination of the neighbor quality and counterfactual neighbor quality. The nqnpn test is proposed as a statistical test to validate a specific interference model. This model assumes that, for any unit in the treated group, its neighbor quality can only be improved by replacing its treated unit with a control unit while keeping other assignments constant. This model implies the absence of interference beyond the Kth nearest neighbor. The proposed method also holds significant practical value as it helps in empirically validating range-limiting interference models under real-world conditions. The work presented here is inspired by and expands upon ideas from Munzer (2020).

Calculations of neutrino emissions from self-destructing dark matter particles within a star are being examined. In the core of a star, the presence of only neutrons suggests that certain types of dark matter annihilation cannot occur via some mediating particles. However, in the dense environment near a star's core, these particles can be produced in pairs, resulting in enhanced emissions of neutrinos when they annihilate into intermediate states of electrons or photons.

The UNIONS project, led by Keck Observatory in partnership with W. M. Keck Observatory and Stanford University, aims to conduct the most comprehensive near-infrared galaxy survey to date in the field of galaxy evolution and cosmology. Specifically, the Weak Lensing Science Experiment (WELEX) component of UNIONS, known as the Cosmological Fixed Imaging Survey (CFIS), seeks to measure cosmic parameters such as $\Omega_m$ and $S_8$ by analyzing the subtle distortions of background galaxies caused by foreground mass. Our proposal, ShapePipe, is a novel framework for measuring galaxy shapes, utilizing a combination of the unsharp mask and morphological ellipse-fitting techniques. When applied to synthetic data, ShapePipe demonstrated exceptional accuracy, achieving less than 0.01 pixel-scale biases in measuring ellipticities and shears for pixels of the DECam. Furthermore, the framework was successfully applied to real data, achieving a total multiplicative bias of less than 0.015 for measuring ellipticities and shears in CFIS's first-year field of view. Additionally, the framework was used to calculate tomographic matter clustering and $f_0z$-binned cosmic shear two-point statistics up to a redshift of $f_0z = 1.5$, yielding an estimated precision of approximately 0.3 percent in measuring clustering and 0.4 percent in measuring shear two-point statistics at that redshift.

A notable result by Weyl and Hermann regarding the distribution of fractional parts of linear functions of irrational numbers is generalized to a product diophantine approximation that incorporates $k$ coprue sequences and a matrix of $m \times k$ dimensions with non-negative integers, as demonstrated in a recent discovery. Building on this, a similar generalized result based on Kronecker-Weyl theory is presented. In addition, a similar generalized result based on Skolem's method was previously published. This study utilizes two distinct approaches: one utilizing Dirichlet's approximation method and the other based on a weak pigeonhole principle.

We prove that for k-rational singularities of local complete intersections, k-Du Bois classification applies. For hypersurfaces, k-rationality can be determined based on the minimal exponent. Moreover, certain local vanishing properties for k-rational and k-Du Bois singularities have been identified. These properties were also discovered separately by [FL2].

We've developed a novel method to create a HEIsing model using a common honeycomb arrangement of magnetic atoms and are capable of simulating its behaviorTK phase through a common alternating magnetic field application in our system. We observed the emergence of the phasTK, characterized by negative effective temperature and an exponentially declining correlation length. Furthermore, our research reveals a direct connection between the critical temperature of the heisenberg antiferromagnetic model and the alternating magnetic field's strength. To our knowledge, this approach for achieving the phasTK through common means is entirely new and the relationship between the model parameters and critical temperature has never before been quantified heisenberg.

Adding two key particles to the Standard Model - axions and sterile neutrinos, offers a potential solution to long-standing problems with neutrino oscillations and strong CP. These particles can also contribute to dark matter in significant ways. However, varying dark-matter compositions of axions and sterile neutrinos present challenges to detecting them. A new research model suggests that the dark matter is composed of both particles, which could potentially resolve some detection difficulties. In this scenario, we examine the dark matter composition and detectability of these hybrid states at experiments like HB21, a proposed heliospheric axion detector. We also discuss how to refine our understanding of the model through future experimental breakthroughs.

This study improves the known upper bounds on how many stabilizer states are needed to express a specific type of quantum state, $d$ magic states of dimension $d$, under the condition that the prime number $p$ is a critical component of $d$. The research shows that the limit is reached when the polynomial $x^{s+1}+x^s+...+x+1$ is divisible by $d$, and it reaches its maximum when the sum of $d$'s prime factors, $s$, is at least 2, and the minimum possible value of $s+1$ is taken. The new findings surpass the previously established findings from Scheringer and Wierichs for specific values of $d$, such as $d=4$, and they match their results for $d=6$. The study also presents specific cases where the new bounds are reached, including when the prime number $p$ is $d^{s+1}+d^s+...+d+1$, and it shows that the new bounds result in a more efficient volume growth rate of $p!^{1/(s+1)}$. The study also considers high-dimensional quantum states and finds that the new bounds grow at a rate of $(\log d)^s$. The derived bounds also have implications for understanding how stabilizer states can be used to efficiently approximate quantum volume. The study also makes connections to research on the minimum number of prime factors of certain types

This research employs the Tsallis holographic dark energy model in two scenarios, 
non-factorizing and quintessence forms, with a focus on the quintessence model.
We investigate its properties by investigating the equation of state parameter and 
state finding parameter using the quintessence model. Moreover, state finding parameter is 
calculated under two scenarios, factorizing and non-factorizing, in order to 
examine the Tsallis holographic dark energy model's dependency on this parameter.
Assuming the Tsallis entropy as the entropy of the horizon, we use the 
thermodynamic approach to analyze its consistency by assuming different values of d.
To assess the model's behavior, we apply current observational data and analyze 
its evolution during different cosmological eras.
By applying a complex form of the quintessence model, we incorporate 
oscillations in cosmological quantities, enabling us to investigate their evolution 
during different eras and determine their periodicity. Furthermore, 
we apply this model to Faraday rotation data and analyze its impact on 
different polarizations of the electromagnetic spectrum.

Between 2018 and 2019, the LAMOST project conducted a large-scale survey on variable and transient objects using four $K$2 plates. This data included 914,519 unique objects at an average of 1.8 magnitudes, with up to five spectra collected for each object. 217,346 objects met the quality criteria for this study. Utilizing an automated system, the research identified 18,720 candidate variable stars and determined their variability patterns. 14,408 of these stars showed clear characteristics of cepheids, eggregars, and other irregular variable stars. Furthermore, the research team manually examined the data to discover 28 novel eggregars and eggregar Cepheids. 30 objects showed signs of novae, recurrent novae, dwarf novae, and thermonuclear outburances on white dwarfs. 44 candidates exhibited characteristics similar to polars, and another 44 candidates showed characteristics similar to cataclysmic variables, including the eggregar dwarf nova. 44 candidates exhibited a significant decline in brightness followed by a slower recovery. 44 candidates showed characteristics similar to polars, and another 44 candidates showed characteristics similar to cataclysmic variables. 44 candidates exhibited a significant decline in brightness followed by a slower recovery. 44 candidates showed characteristics similar to polars,

Previous research has suggested the use of SRAM-based TRNGs for extracting entropy from SRAM's storage cells. Yet, these existing implementations often result in lower-than-expected entropy due to their reliance on SRAM defects, which are not consistently present in all devices. This issue leads to decreased portability and reliability when SRAM-based TRNGs are deployed. This study presents an improved method to enhance both the portability and reliability of SRAM-based TRNGs. According to our findings, SRAM storage cells are highly susceptible to supply voltage variations, which can be leveraged to produce higher quality random numbers without relying on SRAM defects. A practical TRNG architecture, which we call TuRAN, is then developed to improve upon previous designs by utilizing a simplified entropy extraction method and a digital entropy accumulator to efficiently gather a larger volume of high-quality random numbers. We demonstrate the superiority of TuRAN to previous designs as well as improved entropy extraction methods applied to existing architectures.

A preliminary design of a single-electron resistive switch (SRSS) has been developed using two molecules, and its properties have been thoroughly analyzed. An all-trans configuration was found to behave as a resistive switch, and its resistance can be adjusted by applying an electric field. In contrast, a zigzag configuration exhibited a metallic property with low resistance, and transitioned into a resistive state with a high resistance ratio following a transition. Furthermore, the zigzag configuration's reduction energy is 0.043 eV lower than its all-trans configuration's oxidation energy, indicating the potential for nonvolatile resistive random access memory applications.

The concept of loop-tree duality has emerged as a promising approach for numerically computing complex loop integrals, particularly in scenarios involving multiple loops and complex kinematics that traditional methods struggle to handle. To address this gap, we will expand upon loop-tree duality by developing a numerical framework called CausalBosonNumber (CBN) and its associated representation. CBN and its representation serve as an efficient, local way to represent fully differential form (FDForm) numbers, enabling the rapid and straightforward evaluation of multi-loop loop integrals. Its performance outperforms state-of-the-art tools in scenarios involving multiple loops and complex kinematic conditions.

This paper aims to provide a direct and straightforward proof of a specific eigenfunction expansion formula for one-dimensional quantum walks with two possible states, similar to analogous work done on the real line by Hirschman in 1953 and Gelfand in 1960. A more comprehensive mathematical approach using spectral theory was previously done by Nakamura in 2013, but his findings required solving the inverse scattering problem to determine the measure of a specific distribution, which could be quite complex. As an example, we illustrate the proposed method using a non-symmetric non-degenerate Hamiltonian and calculate the desired measure by directly summing the eigenfunctions, yielding a result that corresponds to a non-trivial special polynomial expression, namely the Jacobi polynomial, through straightforward algebra rather than a more general mathematical framework like the Bateman method. This choice eigenfunction expansion formula can also be seen as an alternative form to the Poisson summation formula, namely a result connecting the two is equivalent. We demonstrate this by showing how the eigenfunction expansion and the Poisson summation formula are linked via a relationship between two non-degenerate second-order linear difference equations, specifically one corresponding to the Jacobi polynomial and another to a hypergeometric equation, applying this reasoning to the original non-symmetric non-degenerate Hamiltonian.

This study examines the composition of hybrid stars formed by neutrons, protons, and various other particles. The analysis combines the Sigma-omega-rho model for a specific nuclear phase with two distinct quark phase models, and incorporates Maxwell and Gibbs conditions to understand the phase transition. By analyzing mass-radius relations, a hybrid phase diagram is constructed, and the maximum masses of these stars are found to be within the range predicted by second-generation gravitational waves.

This study examines the behavior of a quantum system consisting of an optomechanical setup with $q$-deformed two-level atoms and a single optical cavity mode, focusing on the Rabi oscillation, transparency, and non-linear effects within the system. As the Rabi frequency, deformation parameter, and phonon occupation number increase, the transparency of the system is enhanced, while at a particular value of the deformation parameter, the transparency remains constant, unaffected by variations in Rabi frequency and phonon occupation number. Furthermore, this research investigates how the optomechanical coupling influences the transparency, finding that strong coupling leads to a minimum Rabi frequency, weaker coupling yields a non-zero minimum, and no coupling results in constant transparency. Additionally, this study analyzes the decay of Rabi oscillation and transparency, finding that increased optomechanical coupling and phonon occupation lead to accelerated decay, whereas these factors have contrasting effects on the transparency's decay.

In a previous study, I developed a model where the Two-Rotors Model's negative scissors states, consisting of two-sided classical bodies, exhibited 1 |$M1$| transitions between 0+ ground states. Building on this study, I explored an analogous scenario with R-parity breaking within the model, introducing a coupling between two rotational degrees of freedom. This led to novel excited 1 |$M1$| states appearing in odd mass numbers, with these states located at the intersection of even and odd mass number states and characterized by 1 beta electromagnetic transitions. Furthermore, I examined how the electromagnetic properties of these states are influenced by the coupling constant.

In ultrathin films, particularly those just a few atoms thick, materials exhibiting magnetic properties suddenly become highly interactive due to a unique phenomenon where some electrons move in a more two-dimensional manner, resulting in unusual magnetic behaviors not seen in their bulk counterparts. Researchers employ cutting-edge techniques such as x-ray resonant scattering, which allows for precise analysis of scattered x-rays, to study the intricate patterns of spin and orbital interactions within these materials. These patterns provide valuable information about how electrons behave in such materials, providing clues to their electronic and magnetic properties. In this context, researchers examine specific materials like La2NiIrO6 and La2CuWO6 to better understand their spin and orbital fluctuations and the underlying interactions governing their properties. In La2NiIrO6, transferring an electron to a particular orbital state causes strong interactions between spin and orbital movements, while in La2CuWO6, an increased interaction between light and matter is caused by increased anisotropy in the material's optical properties. These studies contribute to a broader understanding of how electrons behave in materials and their interaction with light, providing a foundation for further research in the field of interactive materials.

The occurrence of diffusion, both normal and anomalous, is a common phenomenon in nature. In the realm of quantum systems, non-normal diffusion often arises when coupled with chaos. Notably, laser cooling techniques enable the study of quantum systems without chaos by exploiting half-harmonic motion in phase space. This exception holds until the system is coupled with a dissipated lattice, in which case chaos can emerge via a delay in the cooling process. Our research explores the dynamics of N-coupled, laser-cooled bosons in a one-dimensional lattice by applying the therm field approximation and many-body perturbation theory. We find that the system's transport statistics shift from normal to anomalous and back to normal as the temperature increases, ultimately depending on the temperature and initial conditions in the pure system limit.

This study investigates the effects of information dissemination on cryptocurrency markets from the perspective of cryptocurrency trading networks. Specifically, we construct these networks based on simultaneous movements among all traded coins and analyze both pairwise and high-order correlations within them. Notably, we found that the construction of cryptocurrency trading networks relies more heavily on simultaneous movements and less on correlated correlations, especially when analyzing pairs of coins. Furthermore, we found that coins with weak pairs are more likely to form strong higher-order interactions when considering the simultaneous movements of all traded coins.

In a thorough investigation of the impact of zero-point motion on the properties of small molecular cluster quantum states, a novel approach based on the path integral ground state method was developed. A particularly striking finding emerged when analyzing the hydration of a binary acid, $H_2SO_4$, indicating that the vibrational zero-point motion has a substantial effect on the proton transfer in this system, ultimately transforming it from a periodic structure into a delocalized quantum rotor in the gas phase. A new framework for understanding the transition to quantum delocalization in proton transfer systems, rooted in the principles of quantum mechanics, was created to quantify the influence of zero-point motion.

We establish the definitions for a compact perception pair (X, P), where (X,perception) is a compactification of (X,perception), satisfying the following conditions: it meets the requirements of an extended compactification, and every perception on (X,A) can be extended to (X,P). Furthermore, it is demonstrated that (βX,βP) is the unique (up to topological equivalence) compact perception pair that satisfies these extended compactification requirements, where(βX,βP) is equipped with its natural compactification topology. In addition, (M(X,P),d) is defined and shown to be equivalent to ℓ∞(P,X,d') under certain conditions where a pair of mappings h, k constitutes an inverse pair, and therefore it is shown that (M(X,P),d) is separable if and only if the product X×P is compact. Lastly, it is proven that (X,P) is compact if and only if every pair of non-expansive mappings h, k constitutes a compactification, where a compact perception pair is said to be compact when its compactification mapping set is compact. Similarly, we define the maximal perception compactification as a compactification with the minimal set of perceptions which meets the requirements of an extended compactification, where it is shown that (X,P) is compact if and only if the set of perceptions M(X,P) is a singleton.

The way solids respond to temperature gradients is not fully understood from the standpoint of transport coefficients.  By leveraging linear response theory and its concept of effective gravitational fields, it is now possible to derive a comprehensive set of Einstein-like relations that describe this complex behavior. This detailed framework of thermal Hall conductivities includes relations such as Kettner-Casher, Wiedemann-Franz, and Callen relations, all of which are subject to specific conditions. Our approach also allows for the calculation of thermal transport coefficients from fluctuations, which aligns with specific thermodynamic verifications that are thoroughly examined in this paper. These thermal Hall conductivities are then used to study the transport properties of (1) a system of cold electrons in Ising ferromagnets, and (2) a 2D thermal topological insulator, and in both cases, it is found that the Einstein relations are indeed violated.

In various machine learning tasks, simpler models are generally preferred to their more complex counterparts. This paper task is to tackle the fundamental issue of model simplicity by developing a theory of complexity with broad applicability. We created a comprehensive framework that can incorporate multiple models and priors, for instance, by using geometric properties of function spaces to establish a new function complexity formula. This measure is then used in different scenarios, including training deep neural networks and comparing various models of inductive bias, to demonstrate its versatility and relevance.

A new approach for directly extracting the Wilson coefficients of rare $b\to s$ processes is developed using $B^0\to K^{*0}\mu^+\mu^-$ decays within the context of $CP$-violating observables. The proposed method offers distinct advantages over traditional methods based on differential rates. The relevant Wilson coefficients can be determined using experimentally measurable quantities such as direct $CP$-violating asymmetry and angular observables like $A_8$, $A_{10}$, and $A_{12}$, which depend on Bruckner parameters. Since the Wigner rotation can be experimentally controlled, the Buchmüller parameters can be obtained, and the Wilson coefficients can be expressed in terms of these parameters using an expression similar to the standard model case. This approach may also provide a solution to the $CP$ violation puzzle in $b\to s$ transitions.

Automated essay grading has been a persistent challenge in Natural Language Processing, and despite decades of research and improvements in NLP models, there is still much room for progress. One significant obstacle in developing robust NLP models is data scarcity; training data for essays is often limited and fragmented due to diverse writing styles, making them unsuitable for data augmentation purposes. This poses a significant problem, as many cutting-edge NLP models, such as BERT and BART, rely on parallel data for enhancing performance. In response to this issue, we present an innovative data augmentation technique that leverages a transformer-based model to generate improved versions of essays. This novel approach has several distinct advantages: firstly, our method doesn't require parallel data for enhancing the quality of the essays; secondly, our method excels in data efficiency, enabling data efficiency using mini-batches; thirdly, our method yields statistically significant improvements in Z scores compared to traditional data augmentation and training without data augmentation.

Given a simplicial complex defining a tensor's marginalizations, we restrict them to rank one, an idea developed from Kirkup and Sullivant's work on toric models. We delve into the toric ideals arising from such marginal independence models, with a specific focus on models for random graphs and matroids' independent set polytopes. We also explore numerical methods for parameter estimation through both Euclidean distance and maximum likelihood techniques and establish a database for small model examples.

A higher education system or similar opportunities can be seen as a crucial component for maintaining social mobility across generations, especially given that many individuals from lower socioeconomic backgrounds lack access to them. To address this issue, a research paper examines an alternative approach to boosting social mobility by modeling the distribution of opportunities across different socioeconomic groups, with observations consistent with existing empirical data. In this context, policies aimed at increasing the mobility of individuals from lower socioeconomic backgrounds, such as higher education access, can be understood as reallocations of opportunities, potentially benefiting multiple groups at a system-wide level, even if this comes with costs for richer families and their children. To effectively target interventions towards families who can produce the greatest system-wide return on investment, the authors develop a simple theoretical dynamic model and solve for the optimal allocation of resources, ultimately showcasing the potential drawbacks of policies intended to redistribute opportunities without accounting for dynamic effects, such as those that appear efficient in static models but actually worsen intergenerational mobility.

The symmetry of wave functions under parity for particles of opposite spin is used to derive the spin-statistics connection for non-relativistic two-component particles. This derivation does not involve the infinite number of degrees of freedom in a relativistic theory and the concept of a Lorentz invariant vacuum. Although the exchange argument is also valid, analyzing the effect of parity on the internal structure of the wave function provides additional insight into the spin-statistics connection.

We introduce an upgraded RingCT protocol, a signature scheme offering non-interactive, non-malleable, and zero-knowledge verification of confidential transactions, with support for delegated signatures. This protocol supports dynamic sets of key images, thus minimizing the overall protocol size. In addition, we propose optimized approaches for verifying input ownership and ensuring party confidentiality, resulting in a substantial reduction in computational requirements and on-chain data for multi-transaction blocks and delegated transactions. Furthermore, we provide a solution to the issue of potentially explosive protocol growth by suggesting compact representations for hidden addresses and amount commitments, along with a conditional hash commitment protocol that facilitates efficient multi-amount transactions. Our proposal leads to significant performance improvements, including support for high-throughput public verification and efficient private verification, while maintaining secure anonymous verification.

If more specific subclasses of linear systems can be solved in near-logarithmic space, this capability can be applied to solve a broader range of linear systems within a similar space complexity. Our findings build on work by Kyng and Zhang who previously made similar discoveries in terms of time complexity, utilizing reductions between approximate solvers; our own proof demonstrates that these reductions can be implemented using threshold circuits with specific characteristics.

Researchers have made the first detection of three massive gauge bosons being produced simultaneously in high-energy collisions between protons at a record-breaking 13 TeV overcomes the threshold for producing certain rare particle combinations, but measured results, within statistical variations, match a predicted model of the standard physical law, with new potential sources of the phenomenon, such as the interaction of three W bosons or one W and one Z boson at a measurable level, with the most precise calculations of this rare event, with detectors from the largest and most advanced particle smasher at the LHC providing significant insights.

We have initiated the Hebrew Universal Dependencies project by creating a new, expansive Hebrew corpus. This corpus will be used to fine-tune and improve pre-trained language models for further development. By incorporating more varied and contextual data, we anticipate a boost in the models' accuracy, particularly in scenarios where data is limited or contexts are ambiguous. Our work involves fine-tuning a state-of-the-art LLM, specifically GPT-3, on the Hebrew corpus. Notably, initial tests have demonstrated that our corpus enables UD Hebrew to achieve an impressive model accuracy of 93.96%. What's more, our approach has led to impressive results in zero-shot and few-shot name entity recognition and sentence classification tasks across diverse domains, showcasing a remarkable improvement in performance of up to 30%.

We have created a novel method that significantly shrinks any non-compressible subset of an Lp space while maintaining its essential properties. This new approach significantly improves older methods that previously only compressed subsets with polynomial advantages and offers a major reduction in distortion with a lossless compression ratio of up to 2's exponentiation. Our method also results in a compact data structure that maintains the pairwise relationships between points within a constant factor of error. This property can be used to accurately calculate distances between points, either exactly or approximately, by examining their reduced coordinates. This new data structure requires significantly less memory than previous approaches required, with a difference of at least a logarithmic factor. Additionally, we created another data structure that reduces memory usage even more by sacrificing some accuracy in order to achieve an even greater compression ratio.

Recent breakthroughs in machine learning, particularly in addressing cooperative problems, have made significant inroads into multiple domains such as robotics and video games. Cooperative tasks, however, pose a significant challenge due to their intricate nature and are difficult to model using traditional machine learning techniques. To overcome this limitation, a new approach is presented that leverages a coalition of neural networks to collaborate on a task. Each network in the coalition is responsible for processing specific input data relevant to that agent. Through intercoalition communication and information exchange, the cooperative nature of these agents is facilitated. Theoretical and empirical evidence, including simulations of various tasks like 2D environment navigation and 3D object manipulation, demonstrate that this approach yields more efficient agent designs than those developed using machine learning alone. The proposed approach is particularly beneficial when training data for interagent communication is scarce, promoting greater collaboration among agents.

Current studies have demonstrated that degree-degree correlated low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes outperform current best-practice alternative encoders in the binary erasure channel by achieving superior code rates at finite blocklengths. This work derives conditions for density evolution of correlated LDPC ensembles and determines the optimal finite blocklength performance for a specific correlated LDPC ensemble in the blocklength limit of one thousand. The results can be utilized to optimize correlated LDPC ensembles in the blocklength of one thousand and guide the design of correlated LDPC ensembles. It is discovered that to optimize the correlated LDPC ensemble, the given constraints for maximum degree and average degree must each be fully exploited. Furthermore, it is established that the optimal correlated LDPC ensemble is achieved when its trapping set density is minimized.

A novel predictive safety filter is introduced that modifies an unconstrained control signal with a predictive framework to ensure safety constraints are met in complex systems with uncertain parameters. The safety filter is formulated as an optimal control problem that leverages the system level synthesis method to generate safe and consistent control signals. The resulting filter guarantees that all safety constraints are satisfied with an explicit region of stable existence. By leveraging fast online solutions and demonstrating reduced parameter dependence, we show that the proposed filter requires lower computational resources compared to model predictive control methods with parameter robustness, leading to potential real-time implementation capabilities.

A critical flaw exists in the current application of quantum key distribution (QKD) systems, making them vulnerable to the time-shift attack that significantly reduces key generation rates or indicates a breach in the security protocol. In an effort to mitigate this vulnerability, the QKD system is designed with inherent security features such as privacy amplification and error correction, and a proposed solution involves fully phase-randomizing coherent states to achieve absolute security at the cost of increased error rates due to associated noise. However, generating fully phase-randomized coherent states is both inefficient and technically challenging. In an attempt to improve upon this issue, a new method is proposed involving partial phase randomization of coherent states, and an analysis of the system's performance following this approach is provided under the PHQR attack scenario. Although the PHQR approach helps in mitigating the time-shift attack vulnerability, it remains susceptible when the system is under high modulation efficiency. In our experiment, we simulate a DQKD system based on the BB84 protocol with weak coherent states, and demonstrate the vulnerability of the system to the time-shift attack by not implementing phase randomization, resulting in up to 1000 times higher key generation rates without triggering an error rate alarm. In an effort to implement phase randomization, we introduce a new approach involving partial phase randomization of coherent states through a combination of beam splitters, phase shifters, and additional photon sources, and analyze the system's security when the PHQR states are used as QKD signals

Recent breakthroughs in large-scale language models have greatly improved the performance of various NLP tasks, yet the underlying principles of their success are still not fully understood. In this study, we investigate the impact of pretraining corpora on the model's ability to learn new patterns during context learning. Using a few-shot approach, we were able to demonstrate that even negative pretraining examples can hinder the model's performance in learning new patterns. Moreover, we discovered that a two-stage fine-tuning process can mitigate these negative effects and even enhance the model's capabilities in more complex problem settings. To further our understanding, we also examined the model's internal workings and found that a shift in the distribution of latent features occurs when the model encounters novel patterns in context, indicating a shift from its original pretraining distribution. This study not only deepens our knowledge of the effect of pretraining corpora on the model's behavior, but also offers valuable insights into the effective design of new tasks for large-scale language models.

Galaxy cluster observations reveal an unexpected disparity between the energy held by hot gas and the amount of star formation within those galaxies. This discrepancy has largely been attributed to the quenching of star formation through the suppression of two key processes: the rapid formation of galaxies from the interstellar gas falling into the galaxy cluster and the cooling of the interstellar gas within individual galaxies after their formation. The interplay of factors such as radiative cooling, magnetic field presence, and the potential of heat transfer through the galaxy cluster's gas are simulated using numerical models to determine their impact on the fragmentation of the interstellar gas within galaxy cluster peaks. The findings indicate that magnetic fields of 1 microGauss or weaker do not significantly inhibit the shattering of the interstellar gas within galaxy cluster peaks, even if magnetic fields provide sufficient support to prevent the interstellar gas from collapsing into the peak peaks itself, which could lead to a more flat peak in gas density distribution and a more two-dimensional morphology of gas within galaxy clusters. However, if heat transfer of the galaxy cluster's gas is efficient, the interstellar gas shattering process occurs more gradually, resulting in less fragmentation and potentially altering gas morphology within galaxy clusters.

particularly in relation to particles beauty and charm. Mathematical 
formulations related to these concepts are presented and calculated. 
The study also provides a comprehensive examination of the theory's potential 
application in addressing the matter-antimatter imbalance in the universe, 
aligning with the observed phenomenon.

New high-energy string interactions have been discovered in 10D open superstring theory. These amplitudes have unique polarization properties and their counterparts in bosonic string theory are significantly weaker. A remarkable relationship exists among these amplitudes, where one is proportional to the others. Calculations of their ratios are consistent with a prediction made by Gross in bosonic string theory. This reveals that certain high-energy string interaction patterns in superstring theory are unified, unlike the diverse patterns found in bosonic string theory.

To effectively manage the growing number of 5G small cells and their associated data traffic, the concept of self-organizing networks was introduced to minimize operational complexities. The shift from 4G to 5G, characterized by a vast number of distributed 5G small cells, necessitates the adoption of innovative management techniques. The evolution of 5G self-organizing network management is reviewed in this paper, focusing on the architecture, optimization procedures, and efficient resource allocation. The paper also discusses the role of 5G core network in supporting the self-organizing network, as well as the technical requirements for the future of wireless communications.

The objective of zero-resource speech synthesis is to create a speech synthesizer
without requiring any speech audio data. This challenge has been addressed by utilizing
acoustic models trained on text-to-acoustic sequences of non-audio units. While previous
researchers have zero-shot translated images, we present a novel approach to directly
synthesise acoustic units without any audio data. The acoustic units are created based
on a clustering algorithm that considers the coherence of speech units perceived through
acoustic analysis, such as spectral frame likelihoods from acoustic speech models. The
proposed approach involves learning a latent space that text-to-acoustic unit mapping
learns is simplified to text-to-learned speech representation mapping. This representation
is generated without any speech audio data through an autoencoder trained using large
corpora of written text. We evaluated the proposed approach using the written texts from
two languages and achieved successful synthesis of acoustic units of zero-resource speech
samples that were evaluated based on how closely their distribution matched that of real
speech audio data.

Optimizing multi-limbed robots' motion under posture and force constraints poses a challenging nonlinear optimization issue, often accompanied by extensive computation times. We've developed a multi-step optimization method incorporating data-driven linkages between stages to tackle this nonlinear problem efficiently. Both coupling and relaxation techniques are employed to tackle subproblems arising from the partitioning of variables, using QP approximation, and in some cases, solving a initial relaxed problem with reduced constraints and forces to obtain a starting point for the original nonlinear problem. We've tested this method on a 6-DOF robot arm and an 8-DOF robot, with performance benchmarks on various task nonlinearities and restrictions.

We establish nearly precise limits for the probability of converting one quantum state into another using a quantum circuit with restricted unitary transformations. This work has significant implications for understanding the quantum versions of two important concepts, namely, the communication complexity of distinguishing states and the data processing inequality.

We investigated the dynamic behavior of a cup of coffee being carried while in motion, by applying a lumped model that in turn inspired a non-holonomic vehicle representation. The movement of the coffee while being carried exhibits two types of oscillations - one arising from the carrier's motion and the other not directly related, causing the coffee to rise above the level of the cup when it swings in certain directions, but not others. To gain a deeper understanding of this phenomenon, we compared the coffee movement to that of a unique type of pendulum, which自我激发性摆动, by producing energy through side-to-side movements, achieving sustained swings at specific frequencies and amplitudes of this external motion.

In our research, we address the issue of minimizing a convex finite loss function across a dynamic graph in an asynchronous distributed setting. To achieve this, we enhance the conventional variance-reduced decentralized learning approach, specifically DR-DSGD, which is a robust decentralized learning algorithm designed to minimize the impact of adversarial graph topologies and weight biasing. The performance of DR-DSGD is evaluated based on a worst-case scenario across all possible graph topologies. The algorithm integrates elements of the Fenchel dual approach, p-norm minimization, and distributionally robust optimization. The performance of DR-DSGD relies on the degree of the graph's adjacency matrix, rather than its Laplacian, ensuring that the algorithm remains effective even when the graph's structure is unknown. The convergence rate of DR-DSGD under inaccuracy and graph topology constraints is established. The performance of DR-DSGD outperforms traditional variance-reduced decentralized methods in terms of robustness. The performance of DR-DSGD over different graph topologies is validated through theoretical analysis and experimental results.

We utilize the concept of hydrodynamic attractors to establish a universal relationship between initial energy states and the number of produced particles in high-energy collisions. By combining this with an in-depth model of energy release, our findings demonstrate that entropy generated before equilibrium is established naturally accounts for the common trend of decreasing particle production with increasing centrality observed in nucleus-nucleus collisions. Additionally, analysis of LHC data reveals that the ratio of particle production between more and less energetic collisions closely matches the prediction based on when equilibrium is formed and the number of actual collisions occurring, both before and after equilibrium is established.

Using data from the ALMA telescope, we studied the Taurus protostar L1489-IR, which has a bipolar jet moving at around 25 kilometers per second and a less moving outflow, moving at around 7 kilometers per second towards the north-east. This unusual combination of motion, which is known as a countervailing outflow, is seen in only about 10 cases out of over 100 observed protostars. In our research, we used simulations to see if the less moving outflow was a direct result of the angular momentum of the protostellar disk, or the result of the interaction with the jet and a surrounding disk wind. This kind of outflow can be created by the angular momentum of the disk itself, rather than being the result of the interaction with the jet.

This study focuses on developing a nonlinear control method that maintains balance between performance and saturation for a specific class of systems, which have relative degree one and semi-global stabilizability. The proposed approach utilizes a gain-scheduled nonlinear controller, employing two distinct gains in conjunction with corresponding control laws. One of the gains ensures performance, while the other guarantees saturation, achieved through differences in the vector field's direction and magnitude. By leveraging this feature, the proposed controller can simultaneously achieve specified performance levels and ensure saturation constraints are met. The design is validated using a topological argument and an example system demonstrates its effectiveness in comparison to alternative control strategies.

This research provides estimates for the Solar Radiation Pressure as a perturbing force that causes semi-secular resonances in orbital motion. It derives both analytical and numerical resonance estimates, comparing the two methods for evaluating the resonance parameter's value. The study's findings have significant implications for analyzing trajectories of mass particles in the restricted problem, particularly for flight paths of interplanetary spacecraft and the dynamics of celestial bodies, such as comets and asteroids, particularly those influenced by the Yarkovsky effect.

We examine the technique of modeling light matter interactions using a typical Schrodinger equation approach, where the effects of light are represented by a complex vector potential. Our research shows that this technical method is technically correct, yet results vary depending on the representation of the vector potential, particularly when dealing with an infinite periodic system. Representative tight-binding models are analyzed to demonstrate how results depend on the gauge choice, especially when considering both core and valence electrons. For instance, a silicon model that incorporates all electrons shows significant differences in electronic band structure, regardless of the method used, particularly when considering a band that is optically active at a specific wavelength of light. Our technical procedure is documented and illustrated with an example using the maximum-entropy tight-binding technique to predict electronic properties.

Advances in 3D object perception have made it possible to recognize objects
using vast datasets of 3D and 2D images, but this work focuses on perceiving
entire categories of objects rather than specific ones. For example,
recognizing the exact shape and position of a particular chair is more
challenging and important than simply locating any chair in a scene. Due to
the lack of suitable training data and labeled datasets, developing effective
methods for this task has been particularly challenging. To tackle this issue,
the authors create a new approach that utilizes vast, unstructured data from
various 3D and 2D sources to learn object representations and optimize their
structure to enhance scene-based object perception in a subsequent training
stage. They also introduce MEKA-20, a newly developed dataset with realistic
settings for testing the proposed method on 3D object pose estimation. The
results of their approach on both MEKA-20 and existing datasets demonstrate
superior performance over current state-of-the-art solutions. The code and

We will define a confidence area for a sample of size $n$ drawn from a Cauchy distribution, consisting of a combination of a circle with a radius $r$ and a centered square with a side length of $s$, as depicted in Figure 1. This figure shows the constituent parts of the confidence area, including the sample, the square, and the circle. Our objective is to determine optimal values for $r$ and $s$ such that the confidence area minimizes its size while maintaining a specified level of confidence. To achieve this, we will derive an expression for the confidence area in terms of $r$ and $s$, and then find the expression's minimum, ultimately yielding optimal values for $r$ and $s$ that depend only on the sample size and the desired level of confidence.

Conducting clinical trials that involve multiple patient populations face challenges such as recruiting a sufficient number of participants and collecting a large amount of data.  The conduct of trials, such as platform trials and basket trials, is becoming increasingly dependent on establishing shared platforms or portfolios that evaluate treatments across several populations.  In this study, two methods are proposed to calculate the required sample size in trials that involve multiple populations but evaluate distinct treatments, allowing for the sharing of data between groups.  One proposed approach utilizes asymptotic theory, while another employs Markov chain Monte Carlo simulation.  Through the examination of simulated and real-world data from a trial assessing the efficacy of various targeted therapies in lung cancer cases, the feasibility and accuracy of these proposed methods are demonstrated and compared to existing methods, showcasing their practical applications and potential to optimize resource allocation in similar trials.

To satisfy the rising demands of high-throughput in the industry, advanced motion systems must now be designed with a delicate balance between high-speed and high-precision. However, conventional control strategies often struggle to meet these requirements, particularly in motion systems with inherent time-varying dynamics. This research introduces a cutting-edge solution by adapting a sequential loop-closing strategy originally designed for linear systems to accommodate time-varying motions. This innovative approach is combined with a prefilter strategy to enhance tracking accuracy, particularly under constant velocity motions. The proposed strategy is thoroughly tested on a highly sophisticated 3-degree-of-frepsilon air bearing platform, yielding significant improvements in tracking error reduction and increased design flexibility compared to traditional strategies.

We introduce a general, flexible framework called Partial Registration Network (PRNet), designed for automatic partial-to-partial registration of 3D point clouds. Building on learning-based registration methods, which excel at handling complete shapes but struggle with partial observations, PRAdapt, a modified version of PRNet, is developed by incorporating a geometric transformation module and a geometric constraint module. The former extends local features to a global perspective, while the global alignment module leverages estimated pose information to focus deformation and feature extraction on observed regions. We demonstrate the robustness and flexibility of PRNet and PRAdapt on various datasets, including ours, as well as existing ones, by achieving superior results in robust partial-to-partial registration tasks.

A group G is classified as R-infinite if it possesses an infinite number of conjugacy classes consisting of infinite elements. In this paper, we demonstrate that the quotient of a Baumslag-Solitar group G by its commutator subgroup is R-infinite. Furthermore, when quotienting by its second derived subgroup, the group G becomes both torsion and R-infinite. Additionally, the appropriate generalization to nilpotent quotients of type n for G is explored.

Instead of presuming specific new physics will occur at a particular energy scale, let's consider a more open possibility where the SM remains valid up to an arbitrary high scale $\Lambda_{\rm NP}$, with the constraint that it must eventually break down before the Planck scale. In this scenario, we explore how large a particular new physics coupling $g_{\rm NP}$ can be above the electroweak scale, considering the requirement that it must not have already produced observable effects at current collider energies. We then investigate the feasibility of detecting this same scale at a future collider and how various other couplings would behave at that point.

A new technique is developed to process time-sensitive data from ultra-fast experiments using an approach based on optimization in a pathway framework. This technique is successfully tested on data from experiments involving X-ray scattering and electron diffraction to analyze the breakdown of molecules. Results from applying the technique accurately match experimental findings and match other independent analysis methods in predicting molecular structure from simulated data. What's more, this approach is resilient to noise and shared limitations that often hinder the interpretation of ultra-fast experiment data.

We present the results of the first calculations of the longitudinal and transverse light-front distribution amplitudes for several mesons, specifically $D^*$, $D^*_s$, $\rho$, $\phi$, $K^*$, and $J/\Psi$. This calculation also provides the DA values at the midpoint for certain mesons, including $D^*$, $D^*_s$, $\rho$, $\phi$, and $J/\Psi$. The outcomes are in line with earlier literature and may be utilized to gain insights into the longitudinal splitting of a $D^*$ into a $D$ and a $\pi^*$, as well as the calculation of long-distance matrix elements (LDA) for the $D^*_s \to D_s$ radiative decay.

We investigate key properties of several types of Gelfand-Shilov spaces, which are characterized by the decay of their smooth functions and their Fourier transforms. The nontriviality of these spaces, specifically ${\Sigma}^{\sigma}_m$, is proven for a particular case, where $0<\sigma<1$ and $m\in\mathbb{N}_0$, and it is shown that this space is not just containing constant functions. To achieve this, our proof relies on an asymptotic expansion of the modified Bessel function, as well as an inversion formula for functions from the class ${\mathcal{S}}_\sigma$, which is a subset of Schwartz space, and has been proven to be applicable even when $\sigma<1/2$. The study also applies the results to touchtonic Toeplitz operators, showing that a specific space is not equivalent to the whole of Schwartz space and that a particular touchtonic Toeplitz operator is not equal to zero, but rather contains non-zero hypercyclic elements.

Segmenting objects in images from multiple modalities can be a challenging task, particularly when certain modalities lack annotated data. To address this issue, a Cycle Segmentation Generative Adversarial Network (CycleSGAN) has been developed. CycleSGAN builds upon CycleGAN for image-based modal transformation and adapts it for image segmentation tasks, allowing for the accurate instance segmentation of a novel modality with assistance from annotations in other modalities. Notably, CycleSGAN does not require the new modality to provide labeled data. To verify its effectiveness, a series of experiments were conducted on a synthetic dataset featuring a novel modality and an open-source dataset requiring only annotations in a single modality. The results demonstrate the efficacy of CycleSGAN, outperforming a baseline method on the chosen evaluation metrics, including the mean intersection over union and generalized error.

Our proposed algorithm, Feature Mapping RNN, leverages key concepts in machine learning, including parameter sharing, sliding windows, Radial Basis Function kernels, and online learning, to deliver superior performance in current and future RNN-based systems. By incorporating these ideas, Feature Mapping RNN minimizes both training and testing times while outperforming alternative methods on multiple action anticipation datasets, including NFW, Kinetics, and DAST.

A significant UV continuum modeling study of AD Leo's 1985 April 12 major flare is presented. Flare spectra from the UV1, UV2, and UV3 channels of the HUT satellite's beam mode are analyzed. Uncertainties stemming from instrumental issues and variable flux in AD Leo's quiescent NIR emission are resolved to accurately determine the flare model. Flare and quiescent black body temperatures, as well as the flare's NIR slope, are calculated for both the UV and visible phases of the flare. Results indicate that AD Leo's quiescent NIR emission is not related to the UV-emitting plasma but rather consistent with its expected white dwarf surface temperature. A second quiescent black body is also found for AD Leo. Flux from the UV lines Si II and Ca II near the flare's peak emission is estimated and compared with other literature to assess the reliability of the flare model.
